subject: physics
question_text: Explain, on the basis of the law of equipartition of energy, the specific heat capacities of monoatomic, diatomic and polyatomic gases.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 13 Short Answer Question 2 (printed p.139). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The four-way mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: by equipartition C_V = (f/2)R and C_P = C_V + R for every gas; monoatomic f = 3 gives C_V = (3/2)R, C_P = (5/2)R, γ = 1.67; diatomic f = 5 gives C_V = (5/2)R, C_P = (7/2)R, γ = 1.40; polyatomic (non-linear) f = 6 gives C_V = 3R, C_P = 4R, γ = 1.33.

steps.label: The equipartition rule
lines: By the law of equipartition, each
degree of freedom of a molecule
For one mole, with f degrees of

lines.text: U = f × ½RT, C_V = f × ½R

steps.margin_note: Both C_V = (f/2)R and C_P = C_V + R must be stated before using them below.
steps.why: Equipartition fixes C_V from the degree-of-freedom count alone, and C_P = C_V + R then holds for any gas, so only the value of f changes between the three cases that follow.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the R in C_P = C_V + R and just doubling C_V instead.
steps.memory_tip: One rule, C_P = C_V + R, used for all three gases below.

steps.label: Monoatomic gas
steps.margin_note: Both C_V and C_P are needed, plus the value of γ.
steps.why: A monoatomic molecule is a point mass with no size, so it can only move — 3 translational degrees of freedom and nothing else.
common_mistakes: Adding rotational degrees of freedom to a monoatomic molecule. A point mass has none.
steps.memory_tip: Monoatomic: 3 degrees, γ = 1.67, the largest γ of the three.

steps.label: Diatomic gas
steps.margin_note: Name both degrees of freedom: 3 translational and 2 rotational.
steps.why: A diatomic molecule also rotates about two axes perpendicular to the line joining the two atoms; rotation about that line itself carries no energy because the moment of inertia there is negligible.
common_mistakes: Using f = 6 by counting a third rotational axis along the bond. That axis has negligible moment of inertia and carries no energy.
steps.memory_tip: Diatomic: 5 degrees, γ = 1.40 — oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen.

steps.label: Polyatomic gas
steps.margin_note: State f = 6 and both specific heats before the ratio.
steps.why: A non-linear polyatomic molecule can rotate about all three axes, one more rotational degree of freedom than a diatomic molecule, which raises C_V and lowers γ further.
common_mistakes: Keeping f = 5 as for a diatomic gas. A non-linear polyatomic molecule rotates about a third axis too.
steps.memory_tip: Polyatomic: 6 degrees, γ = 1.33, the smallest γ of the three.

insider_note: The three γ values 1.67, 1.40, 1.33 are worth memorising in order — they decrease as the degrees of freedom increase.
